title: KCET 2026 Physics
subject: physics
source: KEA question paper (copy) + KEA answer key column C2 (revised key dated 10-05-2026 applied)

questions.q: An electron falls through a distance 1.5 cm in a uniform electric field of magnitude 2.0 × 10$^4$ N/C from rest. The time taken to cover this distance in second is _____. (e = 1.6 × 10$^{-19}$ C, m$_e$ = 9.11 × 10$^{-31}$ kg)

What will be the total electric flux through the faces of the cube as given in the figure with side of length 'a' if a charge Q is placed at B, midpoint of an edge of the cube (see figure)? [Figure: a cube of side a with a point charge Q placed at B, the midpoint of one edge of the cube]
questions.explanation: A charge placed on an edge of a cube is shared equally by the 4 cubes that meet along that edge, so the flux through one cube is $\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{Q}{\epsilon_0}\right)=\dfrac{Q}{4\epsilon_0}$.

questions.q:
Consider three point charges $-2Q$, $Q$ and $-Q$ and three surfaces S$_1$, S$_2$ and S$_3$ as shown in the figure. Match the entries of List-I with that of List-II. [Figure: two overlapping circles inside a larger circle — the upper small circle (S$_1$) contains charge $-2Q$, the lower small circle (S$_2$) contains charge $-Q$, charge $Q$ sits at the boundary between S$_1$ and S$_2$ (inside both), and S$_3$ is the large outer circle enclosing all three charges]
List-I
(a) Net flux through S$_1$
(b) Net flux through S$_2$
(c) Net flux through S$_3$
List-II
(i) $\dfrac{-2Q}{\epsilon_0}$
(ii) $\dfrac{-Q}{\epsilon_0}$
(iii) Zero
Codes:
options: a - ii, b - i, c - iii
a - iii, b - ii, c - i
a - i, b - ii, c - iii
a - ii, b - iii, c - i
questions.explanation: By Gauss's law, flux depends only on the enclosed charge. S$_1$ encloses $-2Q$ and $Q$, net $-Q$, giving flux $-Q/\epsilon_0$ (ii). S$_2$ encloses $Q$ and $-Q$, net zero, giving zero flux (iii). S$_3$ encloses all three charges, net $-2Q$, giving flux $-2Q/\epsilon_0$ (i). So a-ii, b-iii, c-i.

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor has a uniform electric field 'E' in the space between the plates. If the distance between the plates is 'd' and area of each plate is 'A', the energy stored in the capacitor is
questions.explanation: Energy stored = energy density × volume = $\dfrac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2 \times (Ad)$.

questions.q: In the circuit shown in the figure, the potential difference across the 4μF capacitor is [Figure: a 4μF capacitor in series with a parallel combination of a 9μF and a 3μF capacitor, the series combination connected to a 12V battery]
questions.explanation: 9μF ∥ 3μF = 12μF; in series with 4μF, C$_{eq}$ = (4×12)/16 = 3μF. Charge Q = C$_{eq}$V = 3×12 = 36μC flows through the series branch, so V across 4μF = Q/4 = 9V.

questions.q:
An electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec P$ is placed in the uniform electric field $\vec E$. Then which of the following statements are correct?
Statement I: The torque on the dipole is $\vec P \times \vec E$
Statement II: The potential energy of the dipole is $-\vec P \cdot \vec E$
Statement III: The net force on the dipole is non zero
questions.explanation: Torque = $\vec P \times \vec E$ and potential energy = $-\vec P \cdot \vec E$ are correct; in a uniform field the net force on a dipole is zero, so Statement III is false.

questions.q: A 200 J of work is done in moving a charge 5C from a point A where the potential is - 20 V to another point B where potential is V volt. The value of V at B is

In the figure, the values of currents I$_1$, I$_2$ and I$_3$ respectively are [Figure: 5A enters a junction from the left and 1A leaves the same junction downward-then-left; the remaining current I$_1$ continues right to a second junction where 1.5A leaves to the right and I$_2$ continues down; I$_2$ reaches a third junction where another 1.5A leaves to the right and I$_3$ continues down]
questions.explanation: At the first junction: 5A = I$_1$ + 1A ⟹ I$_1$ = 4A. At the second junction: I$_1$ = 1.5A + I$_2$ ⟹ I$_2$ = 2.5A. At the third junction: I$_2$ = 1.5A + I$_3$ ⟹ I$_3$ = 1A.

questions.q: The number of electrons moving per second through the filament of a lamp of 60W operating at 120V is nearly (e = 1.6 × 10$^{-19}$ C) ______

Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The resistivity of a conductor is independent of its temperature
Statement II: The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases with increase in temperature
Select the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: A conductor's resistivity increases with temperature (Statement I is false); a semiconductor's resistivity decreases with temperature as more charge carriers are thermally freed (Statement II is true).

questions.q: Current flowing through a wire decreases linearly from 10A to zero in 4s as shown in the graph. Find the total charge flowing through the wire in the given time interval. [Figure: I-t graph, a straight line decreasing linearly from I = 10A at t = 0 to I = 0 at t = 4s]
questions.explanation: Charge = area under the I-t graph = ½ × base × height = ½ × 4 × 10 = 20C.

questions.q: In a conducting region, 10$^{19}$ electrons and 10$^{19}$ protons move to the left, while 10$^{19}$ α-particles move to the right per second. The resulting electric current is (e = 1.6 × 10$^{-19}$ C) ______
questions.explanation: Electrons moving left give a conventional current of 1.6A to the right; protons moving left give 1.6A to the left; α-particles (charge 2e) moving right give 3.2A to the right. Net current = (1.6+3.2) right − 1.6 left = 3.2A towards the right.

questions.q: A point charge is placed in a moving train. A passenger A sitting in the train and person B on the ground observe the fields due to this charge. Then
options: A observes both electric and magnetic fields
B observes both electric and magnetic fields
questions.explanation: The charge is at rest relative to passenger A, so A observes only an electric field. The charge moves relative to B on the ground, so B observes both electric and magnetic fields.

questions.q: A proton, an electron and an α-particle enter at right angles to a uniform magnetic field with the same velocity. If R$_p$, R$_e$ and R$_\alpha$ are the radii of circular paths of these particles, then
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB). With the same v and B: R$_\alpha$ = (4m$_p$)v/(2eB) = 2R$_p$, and since m$_p$ ≫ m$_e$, R$_p$ ≫ R$_e$. Hence R$_\alpha$ > R$_p$ > R$_e$.

questions.q: Biot-Savart law indicates that an electron moving with a velocity $\vec V$ produces a magnetic field $\vec B$ around it such that
options: $\vec B$ is inclined to $\vec V$ by 45°
questions.explanation: By the Biot-Savart law, $\vec B \propto \vec V \times \hat r$, so $\vec B$ is always perpendicular to $\vec V$.

questions.q: Two identical circular current loops carrying equal currents are placed with their axes inclined at 45° to each other as shown in the figure. The resultant magnetic field at P is [Figure: two identical circular current loops of radius R carrying current I; point P lies on the axis of each loop at a distance $\sqrt3 R$ from its centre, with the two axes inclined at 45° to each other, one along the x-axis and the other tilted 45° from it]
questions.explanation: Each loop's on-axis field at distance $\sqrt3R$ has magnitude $\dfrac{\mu_0IR^2}{2(R^2+3R^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{16\sqrt2R}$ directed along its own axis; resolving both fields along the x and y directions (axes inclined at 45°) and adding gives the resultant $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{16\sqrt2 R}[(\sqrt2+1)\hat i+\hat j]$.

questions.q: If a paramagnetic bar is brought near a bar magnet, then it is
options: Attracted by both the poles of the bar magnet
Repelled by both the poles of the bar magnet
Attracted by the South-pole and repelled by the North-pole of the bar magnet
Attracted by the North-pole and repelled by the South-pole of the bar magnet
questions.explanation: A paramagnetic material is weakly attracted into a magnetic field regardless of polarity, so it is attracted by both poles of the bar magnet.

questions.q:
Pick out the WRONG statements about magnetic substances (χ = magnetic susceptibility) (μ$_r$ = relative permeability).
I. Substances with $-1 \le \chi < 0$ are diamagnetic
II. Substances with $\chi \gg 1$ are paramagnetic
III. Substances with $\chi \ll 1$ are ferromagnetic
IV. Substances with $\mu_r \gg 1$ are ferromagnetic
questions.explanation: Statements I and IV are correct. Paramagnetic substances actually have a small positive χ (not χ≫1), and ferromagnetic substances have χ≫1 (not χ≪1); so II and III are the wrong statements.

questions.q: Work function of the metal is
options: Maximum possible energy acquired by an electron
Minimum energy required by an electron to just eject from metal surface
Maximum energy which is given to electron to move out of metal surface
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.explanation: The work function is defined as the minimum energy needed to just free an electron from a metal's surface.

questions.q: Variation of photoelectric current with anode potential is shown below. Choose the correct option (V$_0$ = stopping potential). [Figure: four current vs anode-potential graphs; Graph-I rises from a negative anode potential V$_0$ and saturates to a constant value; Graph-II is a straight line passing through V$_0$; Graph-III is a straight line decreasing to V$_0$; Graph-IV is an increasing exponential-like curve from V$_0$]
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.explanation: Photoelectric current increases with anode potential and saturates at a maximum value once all emitted photoelectrons are collected, becoming zero at the stopping potential V$_0$ — this is the shape of Graph-I.

questions.q:
In Faraday-Henry's experiment, a coil is connected to a galvanometer. For the deflection of pointer in the galvanometer, which of the following statement/s is/are WRONG?
The pointer in the galvanometer deflects -
(a) When the bar magnet is moved towards the stationary coil along its axis
(b) When the bar magnet is moved away from the stationary coil along its axis
(c) When the coil is moved towards the stationary bar magnet along its axis
(d) When the coil and the magnet are moved without relative motion between them
questions.explanation: The galvanometer deflects whenever there is relative motion between coil and magnet, so (a), (b) and (c) are correct. With no relative motion there is no flux change and hence no deflection, so only statement (d) is wrong.

questions.q: In the figure shown, the conductor PQ of length $l$ is moved from $x=0$ to $x=b$ and then up to $x=2b$ with a constant velocity $\vec v$. A uniform magnetic field $\vec B$ is perpendicular to the plane of the paper and extends from $x=0$ to $x=b$ and it is zero from $x>b$. The magnitude of emf induced in the conductor is [Figure: a rectangular conducting rail with rod PQ sliding along it with velocity $\vec v$; magnetic field $\vec B$ (dots, out of the page) fills the region from $x=0$ to $x=b$ and is zero beyond $x=b$]
questions.explanation: While the rod is within the field region ($0\le x\le b$) it cuts field lines and an emf $Blv$ is induced; beyond $x=b$, where the field is zero, no emf is induced.

questions.q: In a circuit containing a pure resistor connected to an AC source,
options: Voltage and current are in same phase with each other
questions.explanation: For a pure resistor, current and voltage reach their peak and zero values simultaneously, i.e., they are in phase.

questions.q: A light bulb rated 100 W is connected to an AC source of 220 V, 50 Hz. The rms current through the bulb is

A small town with a demand of 900 kW of electric power at 220 V is situated 20 km away from an electric power generating station. The two-wires line has resistance per unit length of $5\times10^{-4}\ \Omega m^{-1}$. The town gets power from the line through 45000 V to 220 V stepdown transformer at a substation in the town. The line power loss in the form of heat is
questions.explanation: Power is transmitted at 45000V, so line current I = P/V = 900000/45000 = 20A. Total line resistance = $5\times10^{-4}\times(2\times20000)=20\,\Omega$. Power loss = I²R = 400×20 = 8000W = 8 kW.

questions.q:
Match the following Maxwell's equations: (The symbols used here have their usual meanings)
List-I
(a) Gauss' law for electrostatics
(b) Gauss' law for magnetism
(c) Faraday's law
(d) Ampere-Maxwell's law
List-II
(i) $\oint \vec E \cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{Q}{\epsilon_0}$
(ii) $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l=\mu_0\left[i_c+\epsilon_0\dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt}\right]$
(iii) $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec A=0$
(iv) $\oint \vec E \cdot d\vec l=-\dfrac{d\phi_B}{dt}$
options: a - i, b - iii, c - iv, d - ii
a - ii, b - iii, c - i, d - iv
a - i, b - ii, c - iii, d - iv
a - ii, b - iii, c - iv, d - i
questions.explanation: Gauss' law for electrostatics is (i); Gauss' law for magnetism (no monopoles) is (iii); Faraday's law is (iv); the Ampere-Maxwell law is (ii).

questions.q:
[Figure: a ray of light strikes a plane mirror; the incident ray makes an angle of 30° with the normal, the reflected ray leaves at an equal angle, and α is the angle marked between the reflected ray and the mirror surface] Match List-I with List-II.
List-I
(a) Angle of reflection
(b) Value of α
(c) Angle of deviation
List-II
(i) 60°
(ii) 120°
(iii) 30°
options: a - i, b - ii, c - iii
a - ii, b - i, c - iii
a - iii, b - i, c - ii
a - iii, b - ii, c - i
questions.explanation: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 30° (iii). α, measured from the mirror surface, is 90°−30°=60° (i). The angle of deviation on reflection is 180°−2×30°=120° (ii).

questions.q: The direction of a ray of light incident on a concave mirror is shown by PQ, while direction in which the ray would travel after reflection is shown by four rays marked as A, B, C and D as shown in the figure. Which of the four rays correctly shows the direction of the reflected ray? [Figure: a concave mirror with pole O and focus F; a ray PQ travels parallel to the principal axis and strikes the mirror at Q; four candidate reflected rays A, B, C, D emerge from Q in different directions, with ray C passing through F]
questions.explanation: A ray travelling parallel to the principal axis must, after reflection from a concave mirror, pass through the focus F. Ray C is the one passing through F.

questions.q: The incorrect statement about refractive index for a pair of media is
options: It depends upon nature of the first medium
It depends upon nature of the second medium
It depends upon wavelength of light
It depends upon angle of incidence
questions.explanation: The refractive index for a pair of media depends on the nature of both media and on the wavelength of light, but not on the angle of incidence.

questions.q: The critical angle for a monochromatic light going from medium A to medium B is θ. If the speed of light in medium A is V, then the speed of light in medium B is
questions.explanation: At the critical angle, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{n_B}{n_A}=\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}=\dfrac{V}{v_B}$, so $v_B=\dfrac{V}{\sin\theta}$.

questions.q: What range of electromagnetic spectrum is considered as light?
questions.explanation: Visible light lies roughly between 400 nm and 700 nm in the electromagnetic spectrum.

questions.q: In Young's double slit experiment, how many maxima can be seen on a screen (including central maxima) if d = $\dfrac{5\lambda}{2}$ (where λ is wavelength of light and d is distance between the two slits).
questions.explanation: Maxima occur when $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, i.e., $n\le d/\lambda=2.5$. So n = 0, ±1, ±2, giving 5 maxima in total.

questions.q: The radius of first orbit in hydrogen atom is $5.3\times10^{-11}$ m. The kinetic energy E$_K$, potential energy E$_P$ and total energy E$_T$ of electron in first orbit are
questions.explanation: For the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen, total energy E$_T$ = -13.6 eV, kinetic energy E$_K$ = -E$_T$ = 13.6 eV, and potential energy E$_P$ = 2E$_T$ = -27.2 eV.

questions.q: Bohr's second postulate implies quantisation of
questions.explanation: Bohr's second postulate states that the angular momentum of the electron is quantised in integral multiples of $h/2\pi$.

questions.q: An electron transition takes place from excited state to ground state in hydrogen atom, then
options: Its kinetic energy increases but potential energy and total energy decrease
Its kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy decrease
Kinetic energy decreases, potential energy increases but total energy remains same
Kinetic energy and total energy decrease but potential energy increases
questions.explanation: As the electron falls to a lower orbit, its kinetic energy ($=-E_n$) increases while both the potential energy and total energy become more negative, i.e., decrease.

questions.q: An n-type and p-type semiconductor can be obtained by respectively doping pure silicon with
questions.explanation: Doping silicon with a pentavalent impurity like phosphorus gives an n-type semiconductor, while doping with a trivalent impurity like indium gives a p-type semiconductor.

questions.q: In which of the following figures, diode is reverse biased? [Figure: four diode circuits — Figure(1): anode at 5V, cathode grounded (0V); Figure(2): anode at -20V, cathode at -10V; Figure(3): anode at 15V, cathode at 10V; Figure(4): anode at 20V, cathode at -5V]
questions.explanation: A diode is reverse biased when its anode (p-side) is at a lower potential than its cathode (n-side). In Figure (2), the anode (-20V) is lower than the cathode (-10V), so it is reverse biased.

questions.q: A wafer of pure germanium crystal has two parts X and Y. The end X is obtained by doping with arsenic and Y with indium. It is connected to a battery as shown in the figure. Which of the following statements is correct? [Figure: a germanium wafer with region X (arsenic-doped) and region Y (indium-doped) connected in series with a battery]
options: X is p-type, Y is n-type and the junction is forward biased
X is n-type, Y is p-type and the junction is forward biased
X is p-type, Y is n-type and the junction is reverse biased
X is n-type, Y is p-type and the junction is reverse biased
questions.explanation: Arsenic (pentavalent) doping makes X n-type, and indium (trivalent) doping makes Y p-type. From the battery polarity shown in the figure, the X-Y junction is reverse biased.

questions.q: From the graph of angle of deviation versus angle of incidence for an equilateral prism, the refractive index of material of prism is [Figure: graph of deviation δ vs angle of incidence i for a prism, showing minimum deviation δ$_m$ = 60° occurring at angle of incidence i = 60°]
questions.explanation: At minimum deviation, $\mu=\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt3/2}{1/2}=\sqrt3$ for the equilateral prism (A = 60°, δ$_m$ = 60°).

questions.q: Which of the following circuits is correct for verification of Ohm's law? [Figure: four circuit diagrams, each with a battery, rheostat, a fixed resistor, an ammeter and a voltmeter connected in different arrangements/polarities]
questions.explanation: The correct circuit places the voltmeter directly across the resistor alone with the ammeter in series with it, and both meters connected with polarity matching the direction of conventional current from the battery, as shown in Figure (2).

questions.q:
Match the physical quantities given in List-I with dimensions expressed in terms of mass (M), length (L), time (T) and electric current (A) given in List-II.
List-I
(a) Torque
(b) Gravitational constant
(c) Capacitance
(d) Planck's constant
List-II
(i) $[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^4A^2]$
(ii) $[M^1L^2T^{-1}]$
(iii) $[M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$
(iv) $[M^1L^2T^{-2}]$
Codes:
options: a - iv, b - ii, c - iii, d - i
a - iv, b - iii, c - i, d - ii
a - iv, b - i, c - iii, d - ii
a - ii, b - i, c - iii, d - iv
questions.explanation: Torque has dimensions $[ML^2T^{-2}]$ (iv); gravitational constant has $[M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$ (iii); capacitance has $[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^4A^2]$ (i); Planck's constant has $[ML^2T^{-1}]$ (ii). So a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.

questions.q: A car covers the first half of the distance between two places at 40 km/h and another half at 50 km/h. The average speed of the car is
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average speed = $\dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}=\dfrac{2\times40\times50}{90}=44.44$ km/h.

questions.q: Two bodies are projected with the same velocity. If one is projected at an angle of 30° and the other at 45° to the horizontal, then the ratio of maximum heights attained is [Figure: a projectile trajectory launched at an angle above the horizontal, reaching a peak height]
questions.explanation: Maximum height H ∝ sin²θ, so the ratio = $\sin^2 30^\circ/\sin^2 45^\circ = (1/4)/(1/2) = 1:2$.

questions.q: The velocity of a particle moving along x-axis is given as $V=x^2-5x+4$ (in m/s) where x denotes the x-coordinate of the particle in metres. The magnitude of the acceleration of the particle when the velocity of the particle zero is
questions.explanation: $a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$. Since v = 0 at the instant considered, a = 0 regardless of dv/dx.

questions.q: A man weighs 80 kg. He stands on a weighing scale in a lift which is moving upwards with a uniform acceleration of 6 m/s$^2$. What would be his weight in kg? (g = 10 m/s$^2$)
questions.explanation: Apparent weight (in kg) = $m\dfrac{g+a}{g}=80\times\dfrac{16}{10}=128$ kg.

questions.q: A mass M is hung with a light inextensible string as shown in figure. Find the tension of the horizontal string. [Figure: a mass M hangs vertically from point O; O is connected to a wall by a horizontal string and to the ceiling by a string inclined at 45° to the ceiling]
questions.explanation: At O, resolving forces: the inclined string's vertical component balances Mg, $T\sin45^\circ=Mg$, and its horizontal component equals the horizontal string's tension, $T\cos45^\circ=T_h$. Since $\sin45^\circ=\cos45^\circ$, $T_h=Mg$.

questions.q: Two bodies with kinetic energies in the ratio of 3:1 are moving with equal linear momentum. The ratio of their masses is
questions.explanation: KE = p²/2m; for equal p, KE ∝ 1/m, so $KE_1/KE_2=m_2/m_1=3/1$, giving $m_1:m_2=1:3$.

questions.q: A horizontal force of 5 N is applied on a stationary body of mass 5 kg, which is initially at rest on a frictionless table. The change in kinetic energy of the body in 10 s is
questions.explanation: a = F/m = 1 m/s²; v = at = 10 m/s after 10s; ΔKE = ½mv² − 0 = ½×5×100 = 250 J.

questions.q: The angular momentum of a moving body remains constant, if
options: net external torque is not applied
questions.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.explanation: By the law of conservation of angular momentum, it remains constant when the net external torque acting on the system is zero.

questions.q: If the earth were to suddenly contract to half of its present radius, what would be the duration of the day?
questions.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.explanation: Angular momentum Iω is conserved; with I ∝ MR² and R halved, I becomes I/4, so ω (and hence 1/T) increases 4-fold, giving T = 24/4 = 6 h.

questions.q: Imagine a new planet having the same density as that of the earth, but it is two times bigger than the earth in size. If the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the new planet is g' and that on the surface of the earth is g, then
questions.explanation: $g=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$, so for the same density, g ∝ R. With R doubled, g' = 2g.

questions.q: Suppose the acceleration due to gravity at the earth's surface is g m/s$^2$ and at the surface of moon it is g' m/s$^2$. An M kg passenger goes from the earth to the moon in a spaceship moving with a constant velocity (Neglect all other objects in the sky). Which curve best represents the weight (net gravitational force) as a function of time? [Figure: weight vs time graph with four curves A, B, C, D all starting at Mg (t=0) and ending at Mg' (t=t$_0$); curve A falls off gradually and smoothly; curve B is close to a straight line; curves C and D dip well below Mg' in the middle before rising back up to Mg' at t$_0$, with C dipping less than D]
questions.explanation: As the spaceship moves away from Earth, Earth's pull (∝1/r²) falls off quickly while the Moon's pull stays small until the ship is close to the Moon, so the net weight dips below Mg' in the middle of the journey before rising back to Mg' at the Moon's surface — the shape of curve C.

questions.q: Instrument fitted in the carburetor of the automobile to provide the correct mixture of air and fuel necessary for combustion works on
questions.explanation: The venturi-like narrowing in a carburetor speeds up the air, lowering its pressure by Bernoulli's principle, which draws in fuel to mix with the air. KEA's revised key (dated 10-05-2026) awarded grace marks to all candidates for this question; Bernoulli's Principle remains the physically correct answer.

questions.q: There are two wires of same material and same length while the diameter of second wire is two times the diameter of the first wire. Then the ratio of extensions produced in the wires by applying same load will be
questions.explanation: Extension = FL/(AY), with A ∝ d². Since d$_2$ = 2d$_1$, A$_2$ = 4A$_1$, so extension$_2$ = extension$_1$/4, giving the ratio extension$_1$:extension$_2$ = 4:1.

questions.q: In a capillary tube experiment, a vertical 30 cm long capillary tube is dipped in water, water rises upto a height of 10 cm due to capillarity. If this experiment is conducted in a freely falling elevator, then the length of the water column becomes
questions.explanation: In free fall, effective gravity is zero, and since capillary rise height ∝ 1/g$_{eff}$, water rises to fill the entire length of the tube, i.e., 30 cm.

questions.q: In thermodynamic processes, which of the following statements is not true?
options: In an isothermal process, the temperature remains constant
In an isobaric process, the volume remains constant
In an adiabatic process, the system is insulated from the surroundings
In an adiabatic process, $PV^\gamma$ = a constant
questions.explanation: An isobaric process is one at constant pressure, not constant volume, so this statement is not true.

questions.q: The graph of pressure P and volume V of 1 mole of an ideal gas at constant temperature is [Figure: four P-V graphs — Graph-I is a horizontal straight line; Graph-II is a straight line rising from the origin; Graph-III is a straight line decreasing with V; Graph-IV is a smooth decreasing curve (hyperbola-like) approaching both axes]
questions.explanation: At constant temperature, PV = constant (Boyle's law), which traces a hyperbola on a P-V graph — the shape shown in Graph-IV.

questions.q: A mass of 1 kg is executing SHM. Its displacement is given by $x=6.0\cos(100t+\pi/4)$ cm. What is the maximum kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Amplitude A = 0.06 m, ω = 100 rad/s, so v$_{max}$ = Aω = 6 m/s. KE$_{max}$ = ½mv$_{max}^2$ = ½×1×36 = 18 J.

questions.q: A source of frequency ν gives 6 beats/second when sounded with a source of frequency 200 Hz. The second Harmonic of frequency 2ν of the source gives 8 beats/second when sounded with a source of frequency 420 Hz. The value of ν is
questions.explanation: ν = 200±6, so ν = 194 or 206. Also 2ν = 420±8, so ν = 214 or 206. The common value satisfying both is ν = 206 Hz.

questions.q:
Following are statements of a few processes taking place in nature.
I. Free expansion of a gas
II. The combustion of a mixture of petrol and air ignited by a spark
III. The leaking of gas from the kitchen cylinder
IV. The transfer of heat from one heated part of a liquid to the other colder part
Which amongst these processes are irreversible in nature?
questions.explanation: All four processes — free expansion, combustion, gas leakage, and heat conduction across a temperature difference — are irreversible processes in nature.
